 KOIN Portland Follow ‘Sunshine Destruction Act’: UW warns permanent daylight saving time would add 2 billion dark commutes for school kids
 Michaela Bourgeois Sat, November 7, 2026 at 4:30 PM UTC 5 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. ‘Sunshine Destruction Act’: UW warns permanent daylight saving time would add 2 billion dark commutes for school kids PORTLAND, Ore. ( KOIN ) – While Congress considered a bill over the summer to make Daylight Saving Time permanent in the United States, researchers from the University of Washington are warning against the time change.
 According to the UW study , switching to permanent daylight saving time could lead to 2 billion more dark commutes for school children.
 The research comes as 19 states, including Washington and Oregon, have approved their own legislation for permanent daylight saving time, however more states need to join for approval. If Congress passes a permanent daylight saving bill, then the time change would go into effect in those states.
 DON'T MISS: Permanent daylight saving time: How would Oregon be impacted? 
 That bill, the Sunshine Protection Act, however, is stalled in the United States Senate .
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement UW researchers note that school start times are among central issues in the debate because the permanent time change would lead to darker mornings from November to March. While this would lead to darker commutes for everyone, UW researchers wanted to know how this could impact school children.
 The UW research team analyzed 14 of the 19 states that pre-approved the time change.
  Rooftop of Jackie's bar in SE Portland catches fire Tuesday morning  
 Using school start times, school enrollment data along with latitude and longitude measurements, the team calculated how many days every child would be commuting to school in the dark then added the trips together.
 Advertisement Advertisement In Washington, there would be nearly 355 million more trips to school in the dark under daylight saving time compared to the current time change system between daylight saving time and standard time.
 The other 13 states followed a similar trend, with Georgia seeing the highest deviation from the current system, with 71 million more commutes in the dark, according to the researchers.
  7-year-old Newberg boy with Cerebral Palsy scores touchdown in youth football game  
 When researchers extrapolated the results for the rest of the United States, they found permanent daylight saving time would add at least 2 billion more dark commutes to school.
 Advertisement Advertisement Researchers also evaluated traffic collision data, and learned it was roughly twice as likely for a fatal crash involving a school-aged pedestrian to happen during dark mornings than after sunrise.
 "It's called the 'Sunshine Protection Act' because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act," said senior author of the study Horacio de la Iglesia, UW professor of biology.

 "These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It's a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark," de la Iglesia said.
 Advertisement Advertisement UW explained that dark mornings impact everyone as bright light exposure in the morning helps set circadian clocks, which helps humans regulate several facets of their lives from mood to sleep and appetite. Without adequate morning light, bodies struggle to regulate those functions.
 "When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight," said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a UW postdoctoral scholar in biology. "We were asking what's the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school."
  Castle Rock man accused of threatening to execute Cowlitz County judicial candidate  
 The UW study found a few regions that would be hit the hardest by the permanent daylight saving time switch: areas on the western edge of their time zones such as Forks, Washington and communities with early school start times.
 Advertisement Advertisement For example, schools in Alabama and Mississippi have an average start time of earlier than 8 a.m. and both see an increase from about 2 million dark trips for each state under the current system to more than 20 million dark trips for each state under permanent daylight saving time.
 "Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier."

 "For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a.m.," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "That's pretty late, so our calculation (of the more than 2 billion additional dark commutes) is likely an underestimation of the real number."
 Advertisement Advertisement The UW research team warns that permanent daylight saving time would also undo the benefits of having a delayed start time for high school students, which aims to account for teenagers' shifting circadian clock compared to kids and adults.
 "I've heard the argument, 'If we're in permanent DST, we can just delay the school start time to address these issues,'" de la Iglesia said. "Well, if we do that, you will end up going to work later. And everything is going to get delayed. You will get out of work an hour later, and you will miss the opportunity to enjoy your evening light. And essentially, we're just going to be realigning everybody to solar time. That, by definition, is Standard Time."
